content: I'd like to try to get this topic active so interested participants can report on what they are planning on working on / discuss potential future work. (I'm anticipating that there will soon be increased activity in this direction, but we'll have to wait for announcements for details.)

I'm currently working on:

  • an implementation of the LLL algorithm
  • factoring polynomials over finite fields
  • factoring polynomials over the integers (using quadratic Hensel and LLL)

I have private implementations of these, but I'm still writing the theorems about them and benchmarking/improving performance, so I'm not ready to publish yet.

Under the hood these use a (namespaced) DensePoly and DenseMatrix representation, with basic API.

I'm intending to also work on:

  • constructing finite fields (backed by bit-arrays in characteristic 2, and UInt64-arrays otherwise)
  • verifying a fragment of the Lubeck table of Conway polynomials, and a verified search tool for Conway polynomials, so you can construct finite fields without having to bring your own irreducible polynomial

I'm tentatively thinking about (drafting specs, but no code yet)

  • root isolation over the complexes
  • number fields (embedded in the complexes)
  • the field of all algebraic numbers

For all of these components, I will have a doesn't-depend-on-Mathlib computational library, plus a depends-on-Mathlib library proving further correctness theorems and tying definitions to Mathlib definitions.

I would love to hear if others have plans (overlapping, or hopefully otherwise!), as well as concrete suggestions for other things we collectively should work on next (whether building on any of what I'm doing or otherwise).

I have unpublished (somewhat autoformalized) computational models of p-adics, following:

  • [Caruso17] X. Caruso, "Computations with p-adic numbers", arXiv:1701.06794 (JNCF 2017)
  • [CRV14] X. Caruso, D. Roe, T. Vaccon, "Tracking p-adic precision", LMS J. Comp. Math. 17 (2014)
  • [CRV18] X. Caruso, D. Roe, T. Vaccon, "ZpL: a p-adic precision package", ISSAC'18
  • [Doris18] C. Doris, "ExactpAdics", arXiv:1805.09794
  • [BHL11] J. Berthomieu, J. van der Hoeven, G. Lecerf, "Relaxed algorithms for p-adic numbers", JTNB 23 (2011)
  • [vdH02] J. van der Hoeven, "Relax, but don't be too lazy", JSC 34 (2002)

With @Anne Baanen and @Sander Dahmen , I worked on certifying rings of integers of number fields, and for that we used a list-based implementation of polynomials for proving irreducibility over the integers and Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​ (this was certification-based, rather than an implementation of a factorization algorithm).

I’m currently working on other invariants of number fields. But again, not directly implementing CAS functionality, bur rather using a certification approach with externally computed data. Currently I can verify, in principle, the discriminant, signature, generators of the unit group modulo ppp-th powers, the class group structure, and class number of ‘small’ number fields (for example).

With @Pedro Saccomani , @Sarah Azevedo Pereira and @Haniel Barbosa ; we are working on reconstructing proofs from Cylindrical Algebraic Decomposition in Lean. The idea is to have a proof producing implementation of CAD and a module for reconstructing such proofs in Lean. We have done so for the univariate case, following this approach, which we will present on the upcoming Lean's workshop. For the multivariate case we are working on it, together with Erika Ábrahám and her research group. The idea is to have a new solver that produces proofs based on the proof calculus presented in this paper, and then prove the correctness of each proof rule in the calculus. This will require proving the projection theorem in Mccalum's PhD thesis. If this works, we would be able to have a tactic based on CAD to solve goals on nonlinear real arithmetic, with polynomials with rational coefficieints.

Hi @Kim Morrison ! thanks for reaching out, we'd love CompPoly to be used as widely as possible so feedback is very welcomed. I'll answer your questions in reverse order:

  1. I'm a bit worried about CompPoly's choice to have monomial orderings as a typeclass rather than an explicit argument. The whole point here is that there are different choices for monomial orderings, but typeclasses are designed for the situation where there is a canonical choice. Any chance of changing this design decision?

Happy to reconsider this choice, afaict it's not widely used and things don't really depend on it. I'm not sure I understand how the typeclass restricts the ordering, since to prove an instance one has to provide the ordering function?

  1. Is there any possibility of splitting the library into a Mathlib-free part that contains all the definitions and computational parts, and then a with-Mathlib library that makes the connections with Mathlib? I would like to use CompPoly, but this is more or less a blocker for me.

We had considered something along these lines, though I can't promise that it would be done very soon since we're in the middle of building out phase 2 of our roadmap (will take ~6-10 weeks more or so).

Our goal with CompPoly is to implement the basic definitions/API (hopefully reasonably efficiently) such that proofs on the polynomials move into mathlib polynomials as early as possible via a proven ring isomorphism. The mathlib equivalence proofs are already kept pretty separated from the code of the polynomials themselves. Is the mathlib dependency too large to import into what you're working on?

In any case I would love to hear what you're hoping to get out of CompPoly. Happy to continue chatting about this

Derek Sorensen said:

I'm not sure I understand how the typeclass restricts the ordering, since to prove an instance one has to provide the ordering function?

The problem is rather that one has to be careful to keep such instances local, so that other users never get confused about which ordering they are actually using!

Generally with typeclasses, when there are multiple routes to synthesize the same typeclass, it's best if those results are defeq --- which is not the case with your design here.

I implemented a sum-of-squares tactic, following Harrison's paper. (Credit to Heather Macbeth for asking for this since time immemorial, no blame to her for my implementation.) Currently it uses CompPoly, so it couldn't be migrated into Mathlib without the above proposed computation/verification split in CompPoly.

I'm thinking that it would be very useful to have a common library for the basic data structures that may be used here (matrices, polynomials....) and the corresponding API.

Otherwise, a downstream project that wants to use several of these projects, might need to end up managing several similar but slightly different kinds of basic objects (and maybe write conversions between them).

Not sure if this project fits in, but a while back I vibe-coded a simproc to calculate matrix determinants of integer matrices in O(n^3) by scaling up and computing an LU factorization

private def M2b : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ := !![2, 1; 3, 4]
example : M2b.det = 5 := by simp only [intDetSimproc]

private def M2c : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ := !![1, 2; 3, 5]
example : M2c.det = -1 := by simp only [intDetSimproc]

private def M3a : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℤ := !![2, 1, 0; 1, 2, 1; 0, 1, 1]
example : M3a.det = 1 := by simp only [intDetSimproc]

private def M3b : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℤ := !![3, 1, 2; 2, 1, 1; 1, 1, 2]
example : M3b.det = 2 := by simp only [intDetSimproc]

(I suspect it can also work over ℤ[X] to calculate characteristic polynomials)

I'm not actively working on it because it uses !![...] and ![...] as data structures, which as people on this channel have mentioned, is a bit of a pain, and I don't know how to solve this

if there were some computable definition of algebraic numbers

I have some plans here, not ready to announce yet, but I've DM'd you in case you'd like to look at the draft.

Sage (and I think Magma too) implements algebraic numbers as a minimal polynomial together with a complex interval that isolates a root (in fact it is more complicated than that, but the most general the idea is that).

https://doc.sagemath.org/html/en/reference/number_fields/sage/rings/qqbar.html

It can be painfully slow to do certain operations with them, but it works.

However, in Lean you might need to take a quotient of that, because the same algebraic number can be represented in different ways (in fact, the interval is dynamically improved when needed).
(Yes, my plan alluded to above uses a quotient, and has to jump through some hoops dealing with standard forms in order to remain computable.)
